story1126:
In the time before the First People walked the earth, when the world was still raw and unfinished — a place of jagged rock, tangled forest, and water that did not know its own edges — there walked a being of immense power and quiet purpose. The Coast Salish called him dukʷibəɬ the Changer, though he was known by other names as well: Xe'las, Xelas, the Transformer. He came from the East, and sometimes he appeared as a brilliant light moving across the sky, and sometimes as a young man with clear eyes and steady hands, and sometimes as several young men walking together, and sometimes as an invisible old person who saw everything and said nothing.

The Changer walked everywhere. He climbed the ridges where the cedar trees grew so tall their crowns vanished into cloud. He waded the rivers where salmon ran in silver millions. He crossed the valleys where the brush grew so thick that a man could not push through without bleeding. He saw what the world was, and he saw what it needed to become.

The world, in those early days, was full of things that were wrong. There were rocks that sat by the trail and waited for travelers to pass, then rose up and beat them over the head. There were sticks leaning against trees that lashed out at anyone who touched them. There were beings — neither human nor animal, but something in between — that preyed on the defenseless, that spread disease, that brought confusion and sorrow wherever they walked.

The Changer stopped these things. He did not destroy them — the Changer was not a destroyer — but he changed them. He picked up the murderous rocks and declared, "From now on, you shall be hammers. The people shall use you to shape their world." And the rocks became hammers, useful and obedient. He took the striking sticks and broke them in two. "You shall be fish spears," he said, "and the people shall feed themselves with your aid." And the sticks became spears, and the people fished.

The dangerous beings he met — the ones that spread sickness, the ones that lured travelers to their deaths — he changed as well. Some he turned into animals: deer, bear, eagle, the small creatures of the forest. Some he turned into birds that sang warnings from the treetops. Some he turned into landscape features — a boulder here, a ridge there, a waterfall cascading down a cliff face — so that they could never harm anyone again, but would stand as reminders of what the world had been before the Changer made it right.

Every rock, every stream, every bend in the river, every distinctive feature of the land — the Coast Salish understood these as the marks of the Changer's work. The landscape was his story, written in stone and water and the shapes of mountains.

But the Changer's work was not finished when the land was made safe. He sent a flood — a great cleansing water that rose from the rivers and lakes and covered the earth, washing away everything that remained of the old, broken world. Everything living perished in that flood — every animal, every plant, every creature that breathed. All were destroyed.

Almost all. One woman survived. She fled to the top of Tacobud — the great mountain that the people would later call Mount Rainier — and there she crouched on the highest peak, wrapped in her cedar bark cloak, watching the waters rise around her. With her was a dog — a small, loyal creature who had followed her without hesitation when she ran.

On the mountaintop, with the flood waters lapping at the rocks below and the sky dark with rain, the woman and the dog waited. And when the waters receded and the earth appeared again, clean and new, the woman descended from Tacobud and walked upon a world remade. From her and from the dog, the next race of people was born — the ancestors of the Coast Salish, who would come to know every stone and stream of the land the Changer had prepared for them.

The Changer's work established the Coast Salish understanding of the world as a place shaped by a powerful transformer who continues to watch over the land and its people. To this day, the mountains, the rivers, the distinctive rocks and trees of Coast Salish territory are understood not as random features of nature but as the deliberate work of dukʷibəɬ — a permanent record of transformation, a landscape that teaches, and a world that was made, not given.
story1127:
As Snoqualmie Charlie told it, the story began on a stretch of shoreline where the water met the land in a tangle of driftwood and tidal pools. The Changer — dukʷibəɬ — was walking along the beach, as he often did, looking at the world and deciding what needed to change.

He came upon a man with very long legs standing at the water's edge. The man was large and awkward, his body stretched tall on limbs too thin for his frame, and he stood there getting hit over the head by rocks.

The Changer watched for a moment, then spoke. "What are you doing here?"

The long-legged man turned, blood trickling from a cut on his scalp where a rock had struck him. "I am trying to get food," he said, gesturing at the water. "But these rocks — they keep hitting me over the head."

The Changer looked at the rocks. They were the same sort of murderous stones he had encountered throughout his travels — the ones that sat by the trail and struck at passersby. But here they were rolling in with the tide, striking at anyone who stood at the water's edge.

"Give them to me," the Changer said.

The long-legged man handed over the rocks, and the Changer held them in his hands. He examined them — their weight, their shape, their sharp edges. Then he struck them together, once, twice, and the sound that came from their meeting was not the dull crack of stone on stone but a clear, ringing note, like a bell.

"From now on," the Changer declared, "you shall be hammers for the people. They shall use you to build their houses, shape their tools, and carve their canoes." And the rocks were changed. They were no longer the kind that struck at people's heads; they were the kind that fit into a hand and did useful work.

The long-legged man picked up a stick from the beach, ready to use it as a fish spear. He waded into the shallows, aimed at a shadow moving beneath the surface, and thrust — but the stick twisted in his hands and struck him across the face.

"This, too, attacks me," he said, holding his bruised cheek.

The Changer took the stick, broke it in two, and declared, "From now on, you shall be fish spears for the people. They shall use you to feed their families." And the stick became a proper spear — balanced, sharp, useful.

The Changer gave the transformed items back to the long-legged man and walked on, continuing his journey along the shore and into the forest, looking for the next thing that needed to be made right.

But the long-legged man did not remain a man. The Changer's touch had changed him as well. His body compressed and reshaped, his skin grew feathers, his arms became wings, and his long legs remained — but now they were the legs of a wading bird, thin and elegant, perfectly suited for standing at the water's edge.

He became the Crane.

To this day, the Crane stands on long legs at the water's edge, his body poised with a kind of patient dignity, using his sharp beak — the remnant of that first fish spear — to catch fish in the shallows. He is one of the Changer's works, a living record of the day the world was made right.

This is one of many stories showing how the Changer shaped the world by transforming flawed ancestors into the animals and birds we know today. The Coast Salish understood that every creature carried within it the memory of what it had once been — and the purpose the Changer had given it. The Crane was once a man who could not feed himself. Now he feeds himself effortlessly, standing in the place where water meets land, patient and precise, doing what the Changer made him to do.
story1128:
Qals — Mink — is a figure of contradictions. In the stories told along the Fraser River, passed down through generations of Coast Salish storytellers and recorded by Franz Boas from the lips of George StsE'lis, Mink is a trickster, a transformer, a creator, and a fool. He reshapes the world through his encounters with flawed beings, and in doing so, he creates the landscape that the Coast Salish call home.

The longest and most important of the Mink stories tells of his journey up the Fraser River, encountering one strange being after another and transforming each into something new.

It began when Mink tricked a chief's daughter into sleeping with him. This was typical of Mink — he was vain, lustful, and utterly without shame. From their union came a boy named T'qulə'tca, who grew up to become the ancestor of the Ts'uwə'l people. The chief was furious when he discovered what Mink had done, but Mink had already vanished upriver, leaving chaos in his wake.

Near the Harrison River, Mink encountered a woman named LEqyiles — a terrifying creature with a vagina full of teeth. Men who lay with her lost their organs, and some lost their lives. Mink, driven by his usual appetites, approached her anyway. When she bit off his hand, he grabbed her by the hair and transformed her into a rock formation that still stands at the Harrison River — a jagged outcropping that fishermen pass with respect and a wide berth.

At StsE'lis, Mink met a one-legged man who hopped along the shore, gathering shellfish. The man was annoying — he blocked the path, he talked too much, he asked questions that had no answers. Mink grew impatient and turned him to stone as well. That rock, too, can still be seen.

Further upriver, Mink encountered entire villages of people who opposed him — who challenged his right to pass through their territories, who questioned his authority, who made the mistake of treating him as an equal rather than as a being of supernatural power. Mink transformed them all. Some became animals — deer, bear, the small creatures of the forest. Some became rocks, or islands, or bends in the river. The landscape of the Fraser River valley, the Coast Salish understood, was Mink's canvas, and every distinctive feature was a record of his passing.

But Mink was not all power and transformation. He was also foolish, vain, and frequently outwitted by beings he considered inferior. In one story, he tried to steal fire from a chief who kept it hidden in a box. In another, he boasted of his sexual prowess to a group of women who laughed at him. In yet another, he fell in love with a woman who turned out to be a bear in disguise, and he barely escaped with his life.

The Qals cycle demonstrates the Coast Salish concept of transformation as a world-ordering force. Everything in the landscape has a story behind it — every rock, every mountain, every bend in the river — recording where Qals walked and changed the world. But the stories also carry a warning: even the most powerful being can be brought low by vanity, lust, and the refusal to listen. Mink created the world the Coast Salish live in, but he created it imperfectly, just as he himself was imperfect, and the traces of his mistakes are as visible in the landscape as the traces of his power.
story1129:
When the world was very young — so young that the mountains had not yet decided where to stand and the rivers had not yet chosen their courses — there were no people, no birds, no animals. There was only grass and sand and a few strange creatures that were neither animal nor human, beings without form or purpose, wandering the earth in confusion.

Then the Two-Men-Who-Changed-Things came. Their names were Ho-ho-e-ap-bess, and they were brothers of the Sun and the Moon — beings of immense power who had lived in the sky world since before the earth was made. They came to earth to prepare it for a new race of people, and they brought with them the authority to transform everything they found.

The Two-Men were tall and radiant, their skin shining with the light of the sky world from which they had descended. They walked the earth with purpose, surveying the landscape, testing the rivers, feeling the weight of the mountains. And everywhere they went, they found beings that needed to be changed.

They called all the creatures to them — the strange, half-formed beings that wandered the earth without shape or name — and they began to transform them.

There was a creature that stole from others, taking food and tools and precious things whenever no one was looking. The Two-Men caught it and changed it. They shortened its arms and tied its legs together so that it could no longer grasp or run. "You shall be Seal," they said. "You shall live in the water and catch your own fish, and the people shall hunt you for food and clothing." And the thief became Seal, adapted to a life of honest labor in the sea.

There was a creature with a long fishing spear and a white cape who stood at the water's edge, motionless for hours. The Two-Men took the spear and placed it on the creature's face, where it became a long, sharp bill. They took the cape and wrapped it around the creature's neck, where it became a ruff of white feathers. "You shall be the Great Blue Heron," they said. "You shall stand in the shallows and catch fish with your bill, and the people shall admire your patience and grace." And the creature became Heron, still standing at the water's edge, still patient, still motionless for hours.

There was a couple with a huge appetite who ate everything in sight — berries, roots, shellfish, insects — and left nothing for anyone else. The Two-Men gave them strong beaks to tear their food and dark feathers to keep them warm in winter. "You shall be Raven and Crow," they said. "You shall eat what the people cannot eat, and you shall clean the land of what is dead." And the greedy couple became birds, useful in their gluttony.

There was a creature that refused to cooperate with anyone, that hoarded its food and refused to share, that snapped at anyone who came near. The Two-Men changed it into Mink — small, fierce, independent, living on land but eating fish from the shore. "You shall be alone," they said, "as you wished to be." And Mink became the solitary hunter that it is today.

The Two-Men also created the yew tree — a tree of extraordinary toughness and flexibility, whose wood could be bent without breaking. They made it for the people who would come later, so that they could fashion bows and hunt the animals the Two-Men had made.

This cycle explains the origins of all Pacific Northwest animals through transformation. The Two-Men-Who-Changed-Things took the chaos of the unfinished world and gave it shape, purpose, and order. Every creature they created carries within it the memory of what it once was — a flawed, half-formed being that the Two-Men corrected and set right. The animals of the Pacific Northwest are not random; they are the deliberate works of two powerful beings who walked the earth before the First People and prepared it for their coming.
story1130:
In the time before sunlight, when the world lay in darkness and the people stumbled through their days half-blind, light existed — but it was hoarded. A great chief, sometimes called the Old Fisherman, kept all the light of the universe locked in a nested set of five boxes, each smaller than the last, each more tightly sealed. The chief guarded his treasure jealously, letting no light escape, keeping the world in shadow.

Raven wanted that light. Not for altruistic reasons — Raven was never altruistic — but because he was tired of the dark. He wanted to see where he was walking. He wanted to find the salmon streams. He wanted to examine the faces of the people he tricked. Darkness was inconvenient for a trickster.

So Raven devised a plan — the kind of plan that only Raven could devise, involving deception, manipulation, and the exploitation of a grandfather's love.

Raven transformed himself into a hemlock needle — tiny, green, nearly invisible — and dropped into the river where the chief's daughter came each morning to draw water. The daughter filled her cedar bucket, carried it home, and poured it into the family's drinking vessel. The needle floated on the surface, glinting in the dim light.

When the daughter drank, she swallowed the needle. And in time, as such things happen in the stories of the beginning, she gave birth to a child — a boy with dark eyes and a cry like a raven's call. The old chief, her father, was overjoyed. He had no grandchildren, and this child was precious to him beyond measure.

The child grew with supernatural speed, and the chief doted on him, giving him everything he asked for. And what the child asked for, relentlessly, persistently, with the inexhaustible energy of a baby who knows exactly what he wants, was the boxes.

"Grandfather, I want to see the boxes."

"No, grandchild. You must not touch them."

"Grandfather, please. Just one box. Just to hold."

"No, grandchild."

The child cried. He cried all night, his wail rising through the cedar walls of the house, shaking the roof beams. He cried all day, his tears running down his face in rivers, his fists clenched, his voice hoarse but unrelenting. The chief could not sleep. The household could not function. The daughter begged her father to give the child what he wanted.

At last, worn down by the crying, the chief relented. He brought out the first box — the largest — and opened it.

The stars burst free. They flew from the box like sparks from a fire, swirling upward, embedding themselves in the dark sky. The world flickered with faint light — the first light it had known.

But the child wanted more. He cried for the second box, and the chief opened it, and the moon rose out of it like a silver fish jumping from the water, climbing the sky, casting its pale glow over the world.

The child wanted the third box. The chief opened it, and the northern lights — the aurora — spilled out, painting the sky with curtains of green and violet and white, rippling like fabric in a wind that blew from the edge of the world.

Now the child stopped crying. He held the remaining two boxes — the smallest, the most tightly sealed — and the chief watched with growing unease, for he knew that the last box held the greatest treasure.

The child fumbled with the seals. The chief tried to stop him, but it was too late. The child tore open the final box, and the sun — the blazing, golden, world-illuminating sun — erupted from his hands. In the same instant, the child transformed. His body stretched and darkened, his arms became wings, his beak lengthened, and he was Raven again — not a baby, not a trickster in disguise, but Raven in his true form, black as the night he was about to destroy.

Raven seized the sun in his beak and flew. He flew up, up, past the smoke hole of the chief's house, past the clouds, past the stars he had released, into the sky itself. And there he released the sun, placing it in the highest reaches of the heavens, where it blazed forth and flooded the world with daylight.

The darkness was over. The world could see.

This myth — told by the Nuu-chah-nulth and by peoples across the Pacific Northwest in variations that differ in detail but agree in essence — establishes Raven as the primary culture hero and explains the origin of day and night. Light, in the Nuu-chah-nulth understanding, was not given freely by the gods. It was stolen, tricked, wrested from the clutches of those who would hoard it. And it was Raven — selfish, clever, insatiable Raven — who brought it to the people, not because he loved them, but because he wanted to see where he was going.
story1131:
One morning as the tide went out, the old people came to sit on the warm rocks and watch the ocean. This was what old people did in the villages along the coast — they watched the water, they talked about the weather, they remembered things that had happened when the world was younger. The tide was low, and the rocks were dry, and the morning sun was warm on their faces.

They saw a woman walking along the beach. She was alone, and she moved with a steady, purposeful stride. Her hair was long — very long — strung into eight braids that hung down her back like dark ropes. She carried a digging stick in one hand, and she was looking for clams.

The old people recognized her. She was Octopus — not a human woman but a spirit-being who took human form when she came to the shore to dig for clams. Her eight braids were the eight arms she would reveal if she chose to, and her digging stick was the tool she used to pry clams from the sand.

Octopus sat down on a flat rock near the water's edge and began to dig. She worked slowly, methodically, pushing the stick into the wet sand, prying up the surface, finding the clams beneath. She was absorbed in her work, and she did not notice the figure approaching along the beach.

He was tall, with glossy black hair that caught the light like oil on water. His step was light, almost dancing, and there was a smirk on his face that the old people recognized immediately.

"That's Raven," one of them muttered. "And he's going to bother her."

The others nodded. They had seen this before. Raven could not leave anyone in peace. If someone was working, Raven wanted to interfere. If someone was happy, Raven wanted to make them unhappy. If someone was sitting quietly on a rock digging for clams, Raven wanted to make their life miserable.

Raven walked right down to the rock where Octopus sat. He did not announce himself. He did not greet her with the proper words. He simply walked up and began talking — nonsense, mostly, the kind of restless, probing chatter that Raven used when he was bored and looking for amusement.

"What are you doing?" he asked, though it was obvious.

"Digging clams," Octopus said, not looking up.

"Why?"

"To eat."

"What kind of clams?"

"The kind that live in the sand."

"I know that. But what kind?"

Octopus ignored him. She dug another clam from the sand and placed it in her basket.

Raven leaned closer. He peered into the hole she had dug. He nudged her arm with his elbow. He picked up a handful of sand and let it trickle through his fingers. He made comments about her technique, her braids, her stick, the quality of the clams, the state of the tide.

The old people on the rocks shook their heads. They knew how this would end. Raven never learned. He never understood that bothering people was wrong, or that persistence in irritation was not the same as charm. He would keep pestering Octopus until she had enough, and then there would be consequences.

The story — told along the coast from village to village, generation to generation — is a humorous cautionary tale about respecting others' boundaries and not interfering with people who are working. Raven's persistent meddling backfires, as it always does, teaching him and the listener that pestering others leads to unpleasant consequences. The Nuu-chah-nulth version emphasizes Raven's trickster nature and his tendency to interfere in others' affairs, even when those affairs are none of his business.
story1132:
Two brothers — Tihtipihin, the elder, and Kwatyat, the younger — were walking through the forest when they saw something that stopped them cold. A great monster, vast and terrible, with a mouth that could swallow a whale and teeth like canoe paddles, opened its throat and swallowed their mother whole.

She was gone in an instant. One moment she was walking between them, her hand on Kwatyat's shoulder, her voice telling a story about the old days. The next moment the monster's jaws had closed around her, and she was inside its belly, and the brothers were standing alone on the forest trail.

There was no time for grief. No time for planning. Tihtipihin looked at Kwatyat, and Kwatyat looked at Tihtipihin, and without a word they made the decision that defined them as heroes.

They walked into the monster's mouth.

The darkness inside was absolute. The walls of the creature's throat were slick and warm, and the air smelled of rot and stomach acid. They slid downward, tumbling through the dark, until they landed on something soft — the floor of the monster's stomach, where the remains of previous meals lay in various stages of digestion.

And there, in the dim, wet darkness, they found their mother. She was alive — barely — but alive. And with her were other swallowed victims: a fisherman, a hunter, an old woman, a child. All of them had been eaten by the monster. All of them had given up hope of escape.

But the brothers had not given up. Kwatyat, the younger, was the clever one. He carried a knife — a blade of sharpened bone that he kept in his belt for cutting rope and preparing food. He drew the knife and began to cut.

The monster's stomach wall was thick and tough, like the hide of a whale, but the knife was sharp and Kwatyat's arm was strong. He cut and cut, and Tihtipihin held the flesh steady, and slowly, agonizingly, they carved an opening large enough for a person to crawl through.

One by one, they helped the swallowed victims out through the hole in the monster's side. The fisherman first, then the hunter, then the old woman, then the child. Their mother came last, supported by Tihtipihin's arm, her face pale but her eyes fierce with the determination of a woman who had been swallowed by a monster and was not pleased about it.

They all escaped into the daylight, and the monster, its belly torn open, perished where it lay.

The story of the two brothers who rescued their mother from the monster is one of the most important Nuu-chah-nulth hero tales. It is a story of filial devotion — of sons who loved their mother so deeply that they were willing to be swallowed by a monster to save her. It is a story of brotherly courage — of two young men who did not hesitate, who did not argue, who did not weigh the risks, but acted immediately and decisively.

Kwatyat, the younger brother, is particularly significant in Nuu-chah-nulth mythology. After the rescue of his mother, he went on to become one of the great transformer figures — beings who traveled the land, correcting what was wrong, shaping the world for the people who would come after. His first act of transformation was the most important: he transformed the dead monster into a landmark — a distinctive rock formation that still stands on the coast, a reminder that even the most terrible monsters can be defeated by courage and cooperation between siblings.
story1133:
Malahas was a goddess of the forest, but not the kind of goddess that brought comfort or blessing. She was malicious, cunning, and hungry — a being who stole children from their homes and carried them to her remote forest lair, where she kept them in cages of woven branch and fed them on berries that tasted sweet but left them drowsy and confused.

The mothers of the village wept. Their children were gone — taken in the night, vanished without a trace, leaving only a trail of small footprints that led into the deep woods and then disappeared. The hunters searched. The shamans called on the spirits. But Malahas was clever, and her forest was vast, and the children were nowhere to be found.

One woman wept more than the others. Her children — two of them, a boy and a girl — had been taken on the same night, and her grief was so deep that it consumed her entirely. She could not eat. She could not sleep. She sat by the door of her house and wept, her tears falling like rain, her mucus dripping from her nose in long, glistening threads.

And from those tears — from the mucus and the grief — something miraculous happened. A child was born.

He was small at first, barely the size of a newborn, but he grew with extraordinary speed. In a single day he went from infant to toddler, from toddler to child, from child to young man. And as he grew, he acquired abilities that no ordinary human possessed: strength beyond measure, speed beyond catching, and a knowledge of the forest that surpassed even Malahas's own.

The woman named him Andaokut. And Andaokut told her, on the day he reached his full height: "I will bring your children back."

He walked into the forest. He did not need to track Malahas — he could feel her presence like a heat on the wind, like a sourness in the air. He followed the feeling through the dense woods, past trees so thick that their trunks blocked out the sky, past rivers that ran black with tannin, past clearings where the silence was so complete that the sound of his own breathing was deafening.

He found Malahas's lair at the center of the forest — a place of twisted trees and dim light, where the cages of woven branches held not only the children of his mother's village but children from a dozen other villages, all of them drowsy, all of them confused, all of them waiting for rescue.

Malahas was there. She was enormous — taller than the trees, with skin like bark and eyes like knots in wood. When she saw Andaokut, she laughed. "Another child," she said. "Come to be caged."

But Andaokut was no child. He confronted Malahas with the full force of his supernatural power, and the battle that followed shook the forest to its roots. Trees fell. The ground cracked. The sky darkened with the force of their struggle.

In the end, Andaokut prevailed. He killed Malahas and broke open every cage in the lair, freeing all the stolen children. He led them out of the forest — a long procession of thin, dazed boys and girls, blinking in the sunlight — and returned them to their families.

The story from Nuu-chah-nulth tradition exemplifies the theme of miraculous birth and the triumph of good over evil. Andaokut represents hope born from despair, showing that even from a mother's tears, salvation can emerge. The defeat of Malahas demonstrates that even the most powerful evil beings can be overcome by determination, courage, and the supernatural gifts that come from a love deep enough to create life from grief.
story1134:
Of all the spirits that haunt the forests and mountains of Vancouver Island, none is more feared than Matlose. The Nuu-chah-nulth people speak his name reluctantly, if they speak it at all, for Matlose is the most terrible hobgoblin in their tradition — a creature so hideous, so powerful, so utterly without mercy that even the bravest warriors prefer to avoid the places where he dwells.

Matlose is a monstrous being — Caliban-like in his deformity, a thing of nightmare given flesh and hunger. His head resembles something that might once have been human, in the way that a stone might once have been a river — you can see the memory of its origin, but the transformation has been so complete that the original is barely recognizable. His face is a ruin of features: a flat nose, deep-set eyes that glow like embers, a mouth that stretches too wide and is filled with teeth like broken obsidian.

His body is horrid with black bristles — thick, coarse hairs that grow from every inch of his skin, so that he appears to be wearing a coat of dark fur. His uncouth bulk moves through the forest with a terrible, lurching gait, his massive shoulders brushing aside trees as if they were reeds. His hands are enormous, and his curved claws — like those of a bear, but longer, sharper, and black as pitch — are capable of rending prey into morsels with a single stroke.

But the worst thing about Matlose is his voice.

Whoever hears Matlose's terrible voice falls as if smitten. The sound is not a roar or a scream but something else — a vibration that enters the body through the bones, through the blood, through the marrow itself, paralyzing every muscle, freezing every thought. The victim stands rooted to the spot, unable to flee, unable to fight, unable even to close their eyes as Matlose approaches with his great clawed hands reaching.

Matlose lurks in the deep forests and remote mountains of Vancouver Island, in places where the trees grow so thick that even in summer the ground is dark, where the moss hangs in curtains from the branches, where the silence is broken only by the sound of dripping water and the occasional crack of a falling limb. He preys on anyone who ventures too far from the safety of the village — hunters who stray from the trail, children who wander into the woods, travelers who camp in the wrong place.

Shamans and warriors who successfully confront Matlose gain immense supernatural power. The encounter is a test — the ultimate test — of a person's spiritual strength. Those who face Matlose and survive carry the mark of their victory for the rest of their lives: a strength in their voice, a power in their hands, a certainty in their spirit that comes from having looked into the face of the most terrible being in the Nuu-chah-nulth world and not flinching.

The Matlose legend serves as both a cautionary tale about the dangers of the wilderness and a testament to the power of the spirit world that surrounds the Nuu-chah-nulth people. The forest is not empty. The mountains are not safe. And there are beings in the world whose very voice can destroy you.
story1145:
When Old Man South Wind was traveling north, as he often did in the early days when the world was still being arranged, he came upon an Old Woman who was a giant. She sat by a river, enormous and calm, her back against a mountain, her legs stretched across the valley. She was so large that the trees grew only to her knees, and the river ran between her fingers like a thread.

South Wind was hungry and tired. He had been traveling for many days, and his stomach was empty, and his legs ached with the effort of constant movement. He approached the giantress and asked for food.

She gave him a net. "Catch fish," she said.

South Wind waded into the river and cast the net. He was not a skilled fisherman, but the river was generous, and in a short time he had caught a little whale — a small, fat creature with smooth skin and a round eye that looked at him with an expression that might have been pleading.

He was about to cut the whale crossways — through the middle, the way a careless person cuts anything — when the old giantress spoke.

"Do not cut it that way. Slit it down the back."

South Wind paused. He looked at the whale. He looked at the giantress. He was tired, and he was hungry, and he did not see why it mattered which way he cut a fish.

He cut it crossways.

The moment the blade passed through the whale's body, something extraordinary happened. The whale transformed. Its body expanded, its fins spread, its tail split, and it rose from the water like a great bird — no, not a bird, but something larger than any bird, something that blotted out the sky as it rose.

It was Thunderbird.

The creature was so enormous that when it flew into the air it hid the sun. The beat of its wings shook the earth — not a gentle tremor but a violent convulsion that rattled the mountains and sent rocks tumbling down the slopes. The noise of its wings was thunder, and the flash of its eyes was lightning.

Thunderbird flew north and landed on Saddleback Mountain near the Columbia River, where it laid a nest full of eggs. The eggs were large — each one the size of a house — and they were laid in a nest woven from whole trees.

The old giantress followed Thunderbird to the mountain. She found the nest and looked into it. She broke one egg and examined it. "Not good," she said, and threw it down the mountainside.

But before the egg reached the valley floor, it changed. The shell cracked open, and from inside emerged a human being — an Indian. He stood up, looked around, and walked down the mountain.

The giantress broke another egg. Another Indian. Another. Another. Each egg became a person, and each person became a member of the Chinook people.

This is how the Chinook were created — from the eggs of Thunderbird, broken by the hands of a giantess, transformed by the same power that had turned a little whale into a being that shook the earth.

The story also explains why the Chinook, and the Indians of the Pacific Northwest generally, never cut the first salmon of the season crossways. They always slit it down the back, following the lesson of South Wind's mistake. To cut a salmon crossways is to risk transforming it into something terrible — something that could shake the world.
story1146:
Blue Jay's sister Ioi was gone. She had been bought by ghosts as a wife — purchased with ghost-money, traded like property, taken to the land of the dead. The ghosts had come to the village one night, silent and pale, and they had selected Ioi from among the women, and she had disappeared with them, and the living world was poorer for her absence.

Blue Jay mourned. He mourned loudly, as he did everything, with tears and wailing and dramatic pronouncements of grief. But mourning was not enough. He wanted his sister back.

After a year, Blue Jay went searching for her. He asked everyone he met — the trees, the birds, the animals, the rivers — where people go when they die. The trees told him nothing. The birds told him nothing. The rivers, flowing endlessly toward the sea, told him nothing.

Finally, a salmon — old, wise, its scales worn smooth by years of swimming — told him: "The dead live in a town at the end of the world. Go west, past the last mountain, past the last river, and you will find it."

Blue Jay went west. He walked for days, past mountains that scraped the sky, past rivers that ran black with depth, past forests so old that the trees had forgotten they were trees. And at the end of the world, he found the ghost town.

To Blue Jay's living eyes, the ghost town was a place of bones and decay. The houses were made of ribs and vertebrae, lashed together with sinew. The ground was covered in ash. The sky was the color of old bruises. Everything was broken, hollow, dead.

But Ioi was there. She stood at the entrance to the town, waiting for him, and she was not dead — not entirely. She was translucent, like smoke, and her voice was thin, but she was his sister, and she was glad to see him.

"Do not laugh," she warned him. "Do not behave disrespectfully. The ghosts have their own ways, and you must honor them."

Blue Jay promised. He promised sincerely, with all the sincerity of a being who could not keep a promise if his life depended on it.

He entered the ghost town, and the ghosts welcomed him. They gave him food — or what they called food. To Blue Jay's living eyes, it was rot and decay, maggots and mold. But the ghosts ate it with relish, and their eyes were bright, and they seemed content.

When the ghosts went to butcher a whale that had washed ashore, Blue Jay saw only a beached skeleton. When they brought in firewood, he saw only bark and splinters. When they danced, he saw only bones clicking together in the dim light.

"You see things differently because you are alive," Ioi explained. "To us, everything is beautiful."

Blue Jay could not help himself. He kicked the skulls that lay in the street. He laughed at the skeletons who tried to serve him food. He shouted at the ghost children who had no flesh on their faces.

And when the ghosts danced — gracefully, beautifully, in patterns that represented the seasons and the stars and the turning of the world — Blue Jay stood on his head.

The ghosts were offended. The spirits of the dead do not tolerate disrespect, and Blue Jay had been disrespectful in every way a living being can be. He died a second time and remained in the ghost world forever.

This haunting story explores the boundary between life and death and the dangers of lacking respect for the supernatural world. The living and the dead perceive reality differently, and the gap between their perceptions cannot be bridged by laughter or contempt. Blue Jay, who could not see the beauty of the ghost world, was destroyed by his own blindness.
story1147:
Blue Jay and Robin, two brothers, were hungry. They had not eaten in two days, and their stomachs growled like empty caves. They stood at the edge of the creek, watching the water flow, and Blue Jay said, "I will get us food."

Robin looked at him doubtfully. Blue Jay was always saying he would do things, and he often did them, but he also often got them into trouble.

Blue Jay called to the water. He made a sound — a low, rhythmic pulsing that traveled through the surface of the creek like a heartbeat. It was the sound that the sleeper fish makes when it rests on the bottom, and in time a large fish — fat and slow — rose from the depths and drifted toward the shore.

Blue Jay speared it. It was a good fish, heavy and silver, enough to feed them both.

They carried it home and built a fire. Robin, who was younger and more eager, reached for the fish and asked for the tail. Then he asked for the breast. Then he asked for the head.

Blue Jay's feathers ruffled. "You want everything," he said. "You want the best parts. What about me?"

"I'm hungry," Robin said.

"The Q!təə'nse will eat the fish instead," Blue Jay said, naming the great supernatural monster that lived in the deep forest, the one that ate everything it found. It was a cruel thing to say, and Blue Jay knew it, but he was angry.

Robin cried. He cried loudly, as younger brothers do, and then he left. He walked away from the fire, away from the fish, away from Blue Jay, and disappeared into the forest.

Blue Jay sat by the fire for a long time, eating the fish alone. But as the fire burned low and the night grew cold, his anger cooled too, and his stomach was full, and he began to feel the particular emptiness that comes from having eaten well while someone you love goes hungry.

He called Robin back. "Come eat," he said, and his voice was soft. Robin returned, and Blue Jay gave him all the choice parts — the tail, the breast, the head — everything he had kept for himself.

Later, Blue Jay dreamed that people were sending for him to cure a sick person. He and Robin journeyed to the village where the sick one lay — a duck who was choking on a bone. Blue Jay removed the bone and cured the duck, and the people rewarded him with a lake's worth of roots.

Next they cured a wolf girl who was choking on an elk's kneecap, receiving two canoes full of meat and grease.

But Blue Jay's arrogance and greed in demanding excessive payment led to consequences. The people grew tired of his boasting, his demands, his insistence that he was the greatest healer in the world. They chased him away, and Blue Jay flew off, still boasting, still insisting, still unable to see himself as others saw him.

The Chinook trickster cycle's typical structure is on display here: Blue Jay is boastful and selfish but ultimately provides for his family through his supernatural curing abilities, while long-suffering Robin represents patience and humility. The brothers need each other — Blue Jay's power and Robin's goodness — and neither is complete without the other.
story1148:
Ioi had been patient with her brother for a long time. Too long. Blue Jay was a fool — everyone knew it, including Blue Jay, though he would never admit it — and fools need wives to keep them from getting into trouble. At least, that was Ioi's theory.

"It is high time you settled down," she told him. "You cannot wander the world forever, getting into fights, bragging about things you have not done, and offending everyone you meet."

Blue Jay ruffled his feathers. "I am perfectly capable of taking care of myself."

"You got into a fight with a tree last week," Ioi said.

"The tree started it."

"You set fire to a river."

"It was a small fire."

Ioi sighed. "You must select a wife."

Blue Jay was interested. He had never thought much about wives — they seemed like a lot of work — but the idea of having someone to cook for him and tell him how wonderful he was had a certain appeal.

"Where will I find a wife?" he asked.

Ioi told him: he must go to the land of the dead, to the ghost town at the end of the world, and choose a wife from among the Supernatural People. The ghosts had beautiful women, she said, and they would be willing to trade.

She recommended that Blue Jay choose an old woman — someone experienced, someone who would not be impressed by his nonsense, someone who could keep him in line. Specifically, she suggested the recently deceased wife of a chief, who was said to be wise and patient.

Blue Jay went to the ghost town. He found the old woman, and he began to court her, in his fashion — which is to say, he behaved foolishly, misinterpreted every custom he encountered, and acted with the kind of disrespectful enthusiasm that made the ghosts wish they had stayed dead.

He did not understand that the ghosts perceived reality differently than the living. Where he saw bones, they saw beautiful furniture. Where he saw rot, they saw fine food. Where he saw ash, they saw soft earth. He commented loudly on the ugliness of everything, and the ghosts, who were proud of their town, were offended.

He made jokes about death, which the ghosts did not find funny because death was not an abstraction to them — it was their daily reality. He mocked their ceremonies, which were sacred and ancient and not subject to ridicule. He ate their food and pronounced it terrible, not knowing that to the ghosts it was a feast fit for spirits.

Ioi's warnings echoed in his mind, but Blue Jay could not heed them. He was constitutionally incapable of behaving with decorum, and the ghost town was the one place in the universe where decorum was not optional.

The ghosts drove him out. They chased him with sticks and stones and the fury of beings who had been deeply, personally insulted. Blue Jay fled, squawking and flapping, and he never returned.

The story highlights Blue Jay's inability to mature and learn from experience, making him a comic but ultimately tragic figure. It is also one of several Chinook stories that explore the relationship between the living and the dead, suggesting that the boundary between worlds must be approached with humility and respect — two qualities that Blue Jay possessed in smaller quantities than any being in the Chinook world.
story1149:
Long ago, the Great Chief Above made the world. He made it carefully, thoughtfully, the way a carver makes a canoe — measuring, planning, testing each piece before committing to the next. He made the mountains and the rivers, the forests and the plains, the oceans and the sky. Then he made the animals and the birds, and he gave each one a name and a purpose.

After twelve moons had passed, the animal people gathered for a council. They were restless, dissatisfied. Bluejay complained about his name. Meadowlark complained about her feathers. Coyote — who would later become the most important of them all, though no one knew it yet — complained about everything.

The Creator listened to their complaints and then spoke. "Your names are your names. They were given to you for a reason, and they will not change."

Coyote was not satisfied. He complained louder, and longer, and with more creativity than anyone else. The Creator, recognizing something in Coyote's stubbornness that was necessary for the work ahead, made a decision.

"You," the Creator said to Coyote, "will be the head of all creatures. I give you power to keep peace in the world."

Coyote was pleased. He strutted among the animals, puffing his chest, acting important. But the Creator had spoken truly — things were about to become bad.

As the Creator had foretold, the world began to fall apart. Mountains swallowed creatures whole, opening their rocky mouths and pulling animals into the dark. Winds blew creatures away, lifting them from the ground and carrying them to unknown places. The rivers flooded. The forests burned. The animals cried out for help.

Coyote, to his credit, acted. He stopped the mountains from swallowing. He calmed the winds. He rescued the creatures that had been displaced and returned them to their homes. He made laws for the natural forces — rules that the mountains, the winds, the rivers, and the forests would follow from that day forward.

When Coyote's work was done, the Creator told him something unexpected: "I will not make the first human. That task falls to others."

The four Wolf Brothers took over. They were strong, silent, purposeful — everything Coyote was not. The youngest Wolf Brother killed Beaver, and according to the Creator's instructions, cut it into twelve pieces.

Each piece was given to a different animal person, who carried it to a different region of the world. Where each piece was placed, it became a different Indian tribe.

The liver went to one place and became the Nez Perce. The heart went to another and became the Spokane. The lungs became the Lake people. The stomach became the Flathead. Other pieces became other tribes — the Cayuse, the Umatilla, the Walla Walla, the Yakama, and the others. The blood dripped along the way and became the Blackfeet.

This story of the creation of the twelve tribes of the Columbia Plateau explains not only the origin of the tribes but their relationships to one another. They are all parts of the same animal — the same source — and their differences are differences of organ and function, not of worth. Each tribe has its own role, its own purpose, its own place in the body of the people. And Coyote, who started as a complainer and became a lawgiver, set the world in motion.
story1154:
The Transformer — Xe'las — walked through the land making the world right for the coming humans. He moved with purpose, his eyes seeing not what the world was but what it needed to become. And everywhere he went, he found things that needed changing.

Near Lake Chelan, he encountered people who had become corrupted by greed. They hoarded food while their neighbors starved. They took more than their share of salmon from the river. They filled their houses with possessions while others slept in the cold. Xe'las looked at them and shook his head.

"You have forgotten the old agreements," he said. "You have forgotten that the world belongs to everyone."

He turned them to stone. Their bodies became the rocky shoreline of Lake Chelan, their arms reaching out toward the water they had once exploited. Their canoes, still loaded with stolen food, became islands in the lake, visible even today — dark shapes floating on the blue water, reminders of the consequences of greed.

Near the Fraser River, Xe'las found a woman who was something other than human. She had a vagina full of teeth, and she used it to emasculate men who came too close. She was a danger to anyone who traveled the river, and the people who lived nearby were terrified of her.

Xe'las confronted her and transformed her into a rock formation that still guards the river — a jagged outcropping of stone, visible from the water, warning travelers to keep their distance.

In the San Juan Islands, Xe'las found two sisters fighting over a man. They pulled each other's hair, scratched each other's faces, screamed at each other with voices that carried across the water. They had forgotten that they were sisters, that their bond was older and deeper than any romantic attachment.

Xe'las turned them into a pair of islands called The Sisters — two rocky formations that sit close together in the water, visible from the shore, a permanent reminder that the bond between siblings should never be broken by jealousy or competition.

The Transformer also created Mount Rainier — Tacobud — as a refuge during the great flood that he himself would later send to cleanse the earth. The mountain still bears the scars of the waters, visible in the striations of rock and the way the tree line breaks at certain elevations, marking the height to which the flood rose.

Every rock, island, and mountain in Coast Salish territory has a story of transformation. The land itself is a library of stories — a permanent record of moral teachings carved into the earth by a being of immense power and infinite patience. The stories teach people in proper behavior and remind them of the consequences of their actions. To walk through Coast Salish territory is to walk through a textbook of ethics, geology, and spiritual wisdom, written in stone and water and the shapes of mountains.
story1155:
Bluejay is a prominent trickster figure in Coast Salish mythology, particularly among the Chemainus, Cowichan, and other Salish communities along the Strait of Georgia and the Fraser River. He is not like Raven — not powerful, not wise, not possessed of genuine supernatural gifts. Bluejay is, above all, foolish. And it is his foolishness, not his cleverness, that drives his stories.

In one classic tale, Bluejay boasted that he could steal the sun. He announced this at a feast, standing on a cedar plank and squawking his declaration to the assembled people. Everyone laughed, but Bluejay took their laughter as encouragement. He flew up into the sky, flapping his blue wings, squawking louder and louder, getting closer and closer to the sun.

The sun, unimpressed, simply grew hotter. Bluejay's feathers began to smolder. His beak started to melt. He squawked in panic and tumbled back to earth, landing in a creek where the water sizzled and steamed around him. He emerged singed, humiliated, and hungry — which was, in many ways, his natural state.

In another story, Bluejay tried to imitate the skills of other animals and birds. He watched Eagle catch a salmon and tried to do the same, but he could not dive fast enough and hit the water face-first. He watched Owl hunt mice and tried to do the same, but his eyes were too bright and the mice saw him coming. He watched Bear catch berries and tried to do the same, but he fell out of the berry bush and landed in a thorn patch.

Bluejay often interacts with his long-suffering sister Ioi, who tries to keep him out of trouble. Ioi is the voice of reason, the voice of caution, the voice of "please stop talking and think about what you are doing for once in your life." But Bluejay refuses to listen to good advice, and his adventures inevitably end in disaster — for himself, and often for anyone unlucky enough to be nearby.

Unlike Raven, who possesses genuine supernatural power and uses it to reshape the world, Bluejay's adventures typically stem from his foolishness rather than malice. He does not set out to harm anyone; he simply cannot help being himself. He is loud where he should be quiet, brave where he should be cautious, and certain where he should be doubtful.

The Bluejay stories serve as comic relief in the storytelling tradition while also teaching lessons about humility, honesty, and the dangers of boastfulness. Every community has its Bluejays — the ones who talk too much, who promise too much, who believe their own press releases — and the stories about Bluejay remind listeners that the gap between what you say you can do and what you can actually do is a dangerous place to live.
story1156:
Kwatyat is one of the most important transformer figures in Nuu-chah-nulth mythology — a being who walked the land correcting what was wrong, shaping the world for the people who would come after. His story begins with the rescue of his mother from the monster, when he was still a young man with a knife of sharpened bone and a heart full of courage. But it does not end there.

After the rescue, Kwatyat traveled the land. He walked the coast from one end to the other, from the rocky shores of the north to the sandy beaches of the south, and everywhere he went, he transformed the world.

He found dangerous beings — monsters, spirits, creatures that preyed on humans — and he changed them. Some he turned into harmless animals: bears became deer, wolves became foxes, giant birds became songbirds. Some he turned into landmarks: a monster that had terrorized a village became a distinctive rock formation; a spirit that had haunted a river became a waterfall.

He taught people how to fish — where to find the salmon, when to cast the net, how to read the tides. He showed them how to hunt — which plants attracted deer, which trails the bears used, which mountain passes were safe in winter. He established the proper relationship between humans and the supernatural world, teaching the people which spirits to honor, which to avoid, and which to appease with offerings.

But Kwatyat was not all power and wisdom. He had a trickster aspect — a foolish, greedy, impulsive side that got him into trouble as often as his courage got him out of it.

In one story, he tried to catch salmon by building a weir across a river. He was impatient — he wanted the fish now, not tomorrow, not next week — and he did not wait for the structure to be properly completed. The current overwhelmed the unfinished weir, and the salmon swam through the gaps, laughing at him (or so Kwatyat believed). He spent the rest of the day hungry and wet, sitting on the riverbank, muttering about ungrateful fish.

In another story, he tried to fly like an eagle. He tied feathers to his arms, climbed to the top of a cliff, and jumped. He did not fly. He fell into the ocean, and the waves tossed him about like a piece of driftwood until a passing whale pushed him to shore, gasping and spitting saltwater.

Despite his flaws, Kwatyat's transformations established the fundamental order of Nuu-chah-nulth life. The world as the Nuu-chah-nulth knew it was Kwatyat's creation — every rock, every island, every bend in the river bore the mark of his passing. He is sometimes paired with or compared to Raven, who shares the role of culture hero and trickster in a complementary way. Where Raven brought light, Kwatyat brought order. Where Raven was clever, Kwatyat was brave. Together, they made the world habitable for the people.
